scenes.headline: The Spark Executor
scenes.subtitle: The worker processes that run tasks and hold data in memory.
scenes.narration: Executors are the worker processes that do the real computation on each partition of your data.

scenes.headline: What executors do
items: Launch on worker nodes when the application starts
Run the tasks the driver assigns to them
Hold cached data and shuffle files in memory or on disk
Report results and progress back to the driver
scenes.narration: Executors launch on worker nodes when the application starts. They run the tasks the driver assigns, hold cached data and shuffle files, and continuously report their progress and results back to the driver.

scenes.headline: An executor's job
scenes.narration: Each executor receives a task, processes its own partition of the data, caches or shuffles intermediate data as needed, and returns the result to the driver.

scenes.headline: Parallelism comes from partitions
scenes.code:
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")
print(df.rdd.getNumPartitions())  # e.g. 200
# Each executor core processes one partition at a time
df.filter(df.type == "click").count()
scenes.narration: A DataFrame is split into partitions, shown here by getNumPartitions. Each executor core processes one partition at a time, so more cores and partitions mean more of the filter and count runs in parallel.

scenes.text: More executors and cores mean more partitions processed at once — that is Spark's parallelism.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is that executors are where parallelism happens: more executors and cores let Spark process more partitions simultaneously.
